title: Harvest and Cellar
premise: Rafael Lockridge, a property surveyor who has spent five years rationalizing the noises in her inherited farmhouse, is hired to appraise the house for probate—only to discover the house has been appraising her back, cataloguing her secrets in her own sleep recordings. A second voice on the tapes answers questions she never asked aloud, and Rafael realizes the house is counting toward something: a reckoning with the family that buried its crimes in the old well. As the well refills, the dead rise closer to the surface, and Rafael must choose between her duty to deliver an honest appraisal that will erase the family's history, or expose what they did and free the voices trapped below. In the end she burns the appraisal, opens the well herself, and lets the count finish—but the final recording captures three voices now, and one of them is hers.
about_author: Coral Joubert is the pen name of a former rural land assessor who spent a decade walking the property lines of abandoned homesteads across the American South. Her fiction draws on court records, probate disputes, and the things land remembers when no one is left to lie about it.

chapters.title: The Appraisal Clause
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. She accepts a probate appraisal of the Lockridge farmhouse—the house she fled five years ago—telling herself the money justifies returning. The emotional beat is brittle denial: she measures every room twice, as if precision could keep the past at arm's length.

chapters.title: Baseline Noise
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Setting up her sleep-recording rig out of old habit, she documents settling sounds, wind in the chimney, pipes knocking. The beat is false comfort: everything gets an explanation, and she writes each one down like evidence for a case she's losing to herself.

chapters.title: Square Footage
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Measuring the cellar, her laser level returns readings that don't close—a room longer than the footprint allows. She finds fresh scratch marks inside the well cap. The beat is the first crack: professional certainty meets a number that cannot be argued away.

chapters.title: Questions in the Dark
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Reviewing night three's audio, she hears a second voice beneath her sleep-talk, answering questions she never asked: 'Who counted you?' The beat is vertigo—she plays it eleven times, and by the eleventh, she's whispering along.

chapters.title: The Estate of Mireille Lockridge
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: letters from the deceased aunt Mireille, read against Rafael's daylight inspection. The aunt documented 'the count' reaching forty-one in 1987. The beat is dread through bureaucracy—inherited paperwork becomes a horror archive.

chapters.title: Chain of Title
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV at the county records office. Deeds show the house sold four times, each owner dying within a year of sale; a fifth deed from 1911 names a family erased from every other record. The beat is obsession kindling—she skips lunch, then dinner, then sleep.

chapters.title: What the Well Remembers
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. She pries the well cap and smells water where there should be dust; the waterline has risen six inches since chapter three. A voice asks, clearly now: 'Are you the counter?' The beat is terror sharpening into purpose.

chapters.title: Duty Calls Collect
chapters.summary: POV of Dana Whitfield, the estate attorney, pressuring Rafael by phone to finalize the appraisal before the family contest deadline. The beat is external pressure tightening—Rafael lies smoothly about progress and hates how easily it comes.

chapters.title: Sleep Study
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. She begins asking the voice questions deliberately before bed. It answers with dates, names, and one instruction: 'Get them out ahead of the count.' The beat is uneasy alliance—she's negotiating with whatever lives in her recordings.

chapters.title: The Family Arrives
chapters.summary: Multi-POV: cousins Odile and Marcus Lockridge arrive to dispute the will, all charm and litigation threats. Rafael watches the house react—doors swelling shut, lights browning. The beat is performance and menace: everyone lying, everyone heard.

chapters.title: Forty-One
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Exploring the cellar alone, she finds her grandmother's tally wall behind drywall—forty-one marks, and a forty-second half-carved. The beat is inherited guilt surfacing; she flees upstairs and says nothing, which the house notes.

chapters.title: Refill
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. The well water reaches the lip overnight. The voice explains: when the well fills completely, the count completes, and what was put down comes up. The beat is a deadline made physical—she can hear water rising under the floors.

chapters.title: Love Against Duty
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Marcus, softened and scared, confesses the family knew and paid to keep it quiet; he offers Rafael a bribe to sign the clean appraisal. She almost takes it—for the first time we see why she stayed invisible so long. The beat is temptation with a human face.

chapters.title: The Erased Fifth Family
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV, archival. She reconstructs the 1911 deed: the Boudreaux family, sharecroppers the Lockridges drowned in the well after a wage dispute, their names struck from records by a judge on the payroll. The beat is grief and fury—justice outside the law begins here.

chapters.title: Contested Ground
chapters.summary: Dana Whitfield's POV. The attorney arrives in person, finds Rafael's research, and threatens to have her declared incompetent to appraise. The beat is institutional power versus truth—paperwork weaponized, and Rafael's professional identity hanging by a thread.

chapters.title: Night Count
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. All three living Lockridges sleep in the house; the recordings capture five voices answering questions, including Odile admitting what she saw. The count stands at forty-one and rising. The beat is claustrophobic convergence—everyone's secrets on one tape.

chapters.title: What Appraises Back
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. The house turns her own methods against her: measurements rearrange, her survey maps redraw themselves into a diagram of the well, and her name appears on the tally wall. The beat is identity collapse—she is not the surveyor but the surveyed.

chapters.title: Evacuation
chapters.summary: Marcus and Odile POVs. Rafael tells them everything and orders them out before dawn; Marcus refuses to leave without the deed, Odile refuses to leave Rafael. The beat is love against duty fracturing the family along new lines—loyalty rerouted.

chapters.title: The Count Completes
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV, alone at the well at dawn. The water crests; the dead Boudreaux family surfaces as figures in the water, patient, waiting for acknowledgment rather than revenge. The beat is terrible awe—horror transfigured into reckoning.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Instead of filing the clean appraisal, she files the recordings, the deeds, and her sworn account with the county—justice outside the law, delivered through the only channel she has. The beat is costly courage: she torches her career to give the dead their names back.

chapters.title: Closing the Estate
chapters.summary: Multi-POV resolution. The well drains to mud and bones; police excavate; Odile testifies, Marcus disappears with his bribe conscience intact, Dana resigns. Rafael buries the Boudreaux names in a proper register. The beat is exhausted, imperfect peace.

chapters.title: Three Voices
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV, epilogue. Months later, in her new apartment, she reviews an old tape out of habit and hears three voices: the questioner, the answerer, and a third—herself—asking 'Who counts you now?' The beat is open-ended haunting: identity unresolved, the story listening back.
